fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that we don't have a good way to measure it yet, and the measurements we do have are not very encouraging.

Let me start with a simple experiment we did a couple of years ago. We took three of the biggest web-scale image datasets at the time, YFCC, CC, and DataComp, and we trained a classifier to predict which dataset an image came from. If these datasets were really "the internet" in some broad, neutral sense, you'd expect that task to be nearly impossible. Instead, a standard ConvNet got well above eighty percent accuracy on three-way classification. And it kept getting better with more training data, so it wasn't memorization. Each of these datasets has its own signature. The way they were crawled, the filtering, the captions, the platforms they came from, all of that leaves a fingerprint that a model can pick up on. So scale alone did not wash out the bias. That was the whole premise of the dataset bias debate from a decade earlier, and it turns out we're still there.

So when people say "internet-scale," I'd push back on the word itself. These datasets are not samples of the world. They're samples of what people chose to photograph, upload, and caption, filtered through whatever heuristics the dataset builders used. That distribution is extremely peaked. There are millions of cats and food photos, and comparatively very little of microscopy, satellite imagery, industrial inspection, surgical video, or anything a robot's wrist camera sees. The breadth is very uneven even if the count is huge.

How do I actually assess it in practice? A few things. First, I look at how performance scales on a target domain as you add more web data. If you double the pretraining data and the downstream task in, say, pathology barely moves, that tells you the data you're adding isn't covering that part of the space. Second, I like holding out entire domains rather than random samples. Random test splits from the same distribution will always look great. Holding out a domain tells you whether the representation actually transfers or whether the model is just interpolating. Third, that dataset classification trick is a nice bias meter. If a model can easily tell your data apart from some other source, your data has a signature, and a signature means there's something it's not covering.

I'd also add one caveat about "every task." Vision is not one task. Classification, dense prediction, geometry, video, all of those stress different parts of what the model has learned. We've seen that models that look amazing on linear probing or zero-shot ImageNet can still be mediocre at things like depth or fine-grained localization. So even within the data we have, broad in one axis doesn't mean broad in another.

My overall view is that web data is a fantastic starting point and we should use it, but I'm skeptical that it gets us to universal generalization on its own. The more likely path is web pretraining plus deliberate, targeted data collection for the parts of the world the internet doesn't photograph. And being honest about where the gaps are is the first step, which is why I think these measurement questions are underrated compared to just scaling.

opus-5.5.text:
I'd say it's hard to assess directly, and "every task" is a very high bar. There isn't a single number that tells you a dataset is broad enough. So I mostly look at it indirectly, from a few angles.

One experiment I like is what we called dataset classification. A decade ago, Torralba and Efros showed you could train a classifier to tell which dataset an image came from, like ImageNet versus Caltech versus PASCAL. That told you those datasets were biased, each with its own "signature." The hope with internet-scale data was that this problem would mostly go away. If you scrape billions of images from the web, surely they all start to look like samples from the same visual world.

So we tested that. We took several large, supposedly very diverse web datasets, like YFCC, Conceptual Captions, DataComp and LAION. We trained a network to predict which dataset each image came from. To a human, these images look basically interchangeable. You'd do close to chance. But the network gets very high accuracy, something like eighty percent on a three-way split. It also isn't just memorizing, because it generalizes to held-out images. That tells you each of these "internet-scale" datasets still occupies its own corner of the visual distribution. Each one carries traces of how it was collected, filtered and curated. So even at that scale, we're not sampling the visual world uniformly.

The second angle is looking at failures rather than averages. Models trained on this data can look great on standard benchmarks and still be weirdly blind to simple things. In some of our work on CLIP-style encoders, they struggled with orientation, counting, viewpoint and small spatial details. Those things just aren't emphasized in image–caption pairs from the web. People rarely write "the dog is facing left" in an alt-text. So the data covers lots of semantic concepts, but some visual properties are underrepresented, and the models inherit that.

The third angle is just asking where the images come from. Internet images are mostly photos that humans chose to take and upload. They're framed nicely, the object is usually in the center, the lighting is decent, and the subjects are things people find interesting. That's very different from what a robot's camera sees, or from egocentric video, medical scans, satellite imagery or industrial inspection. For those domains, web data gives you a useful prior, but it's not sufficient on its own.

So my honest answer is that these datasets are broad enough to give you very strong general-purpose representations. That's a real achievement, and it's why foundation models transfer so well. But "generalize to every task" is not something we can claim. The dataset classification result shows the coverage is still uneven. And the failure cases show there are whole dimensions of visual understanding the data barely touches. The way forward is probably not just more of the same scraped data. It's being more deliberate about what kinds of visual experience are missing, and adding those in.

fable-5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly I think the answer right now is: we don't really know, and we don't have great ways to measure it.

Let me start with a comparison to language, because I think it's instructive. In NLP, the internet is in some sense a direct dump of what we care about — people write text to communicate knowledge, so when you scrape the web you're getting the actual target distribution. Vision is different. Internet images are what people chose to photograph and upload, so the distribution is heavily skewed toward certain things — people, pets, food, landmarks, product photos. It's broad, but it's broad in a very particular, human-curated way.

So when I think about whether it's "enough," I like to break it down by what kind of task you're asking about. For recognition-style tasks on natural images — classification, detection, retrieval of everyday scenes — I'd say we're close to saturated. Models trained on web-scale data like CLIP-style models transfer remarkably well there, and adding more of the same data gives you diminishing returns. But the moment you move to domains that are underrepresented on the internet — medical imaging, satellite and aerial views, microscopy, industrial inspection, egocentric video from a robot's perspective — the coverage drops off a cliff. Those images exist in the world in enormous quantities, but they don't get uploaded to the web, or they're locked behind privacy and institutional barriers.

In practice, the way I assess this is empirical rather than theoretical. You take a frozen pretrained model and probe it across a deliberately diverse suite of downstream tasks, and you watch where transfer performance falls apart. The failure modes tell you where the pretraining distribution is thin. What's interesting is that scale alone doesn't fix this — going from two billion to ten billion web images mostly gives you more of the same modes. The marginal image is redundant. So I'd argue diversity matters more than raw count at this point, and our benchmarks are actually part of the problem, because most of them are themselves drawn from the same internet distribution. We may be overestimating generality because we're testing in-distribution without realizing it.

There's also a deeper issue, which is that "every task" in vision includes things that aren't really about semantics at all — 3D geometry, physics, fine-grained spatial reasoning, dynamics over time. Static internet photos are a pretty impoverished signal for those. So my honest take is: internet-scale image data is sufficient for a surprisingly large slice of semantic vision tasks, but it's not sufficient for vision as a whole, and the gap won't be closed by scraping harder. It'll be closed by video, by embodied data collection, by synthetic data, and by actually going out and gathering the distributions the internet doesn't give us for free.

opus-5.text:
I don't think you can settle that by argument — you have to turn it into an experiment. The one we ran is almost embarrassingly simple. Take three large-scale datasets — YFCC, CC, DataComp, say — sample an equal number of images from each, strip the labels, and train a model to predict which dataset each image came from. If these were all just unbiased samples from "the visual world," the task should be impossible. You'd get chance, 33%.

We got about 84% on held-out images. And it's not memorization — the model generalizes to images it has never seen, it works with heavy augmentation, it works if you only show it a small crop. Humans, when we tried this, do much worse than the model, around 40-45%. So the model is picking up on something real and fairly semantic about each dataset's character that we can't even articulate. These are curated, hundreds of millions of images, and they still have a signature you can read off a single photo. Scale did not wash the bias out.

So as a proxy for your question — are they broad enough? — the answer is pretty clearly no. They're each a distinctive slice.

And there's a deeper issue, which is that all of them are drawn from the same meta-distribution: images people chose to photograph and upload. That's a very particular sampling of reality. Nobody uploads the view from a robot's wrist camera, or a factory floor at 3 a.m., or the underside of their sink. The boring, the occluded, the badly lit, the rare failure case — those are systematically missing, and no amount of scraping more internet fixes it.

The honest epistemic position is that we only discover a dataset was too narrow after a model fails at a task we happened to think of testing. So I'm skeptical of anyone claiming breadth in the absolute. What I think is actually tractable is measuring it relatively — can you tell sources apart, does training on A transfer to B, how big is the gap. Those numbers you can put on a slide.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I'd start by pushing back on "every task." I don't think any internet-scale dataset is broad enough for that, and the question is how you would even measure it. One experiment we ran was a "name that dataset" game. Take images from big datasets like YFCC, CC12M, and DataComp, which are all huge and all scraped from the internet, and train a neural network to predict which dataset an image came from. If the datasets were truly diverse and representative of the visual world, they should look statistically alike and this should be close to chance. But the classifier gets well above 80% accuracy on a three-way split. So each dataset has its own signature, whether in style, in the filtering pipeline, or in what people upload. They are not just random samples of the visual world.

The other issue is that internet data is biased toward what people choose to photograph and post. You see lots of food, pets, landmarks, and products. You see much less of the long tail, like industrial settings, many scientific and medical domains, or egocentric and robotic viewpoints. So scale doesn't automatically give you breadth.

In practice, the way to assess it is empirical: test on out-of-distribution tasks and see where the model breaks, rather than assuming the dataset covers everything.

haiku-5.5.text:
I don't think there's a clean answer, and I'd be wary of anyone who says there is. "Broad" is doing a lot of work in that question. Internet-scale data covers an enormous range of visual content, but coverage of images isn't the same as coverage of tasks. A model can see billions of photos and still have thin support for precise geometry, fine-grained spatial reasoning, or anything that's rare in how people photograph and caption the world.

The way I try to assess it is by looking at where models fail rather than at how big the dataset is. When you test a model trained on web-scale data under distribution shift, like different domains, sensor setups, or tasks that need exact structure, the gaps show up quickly. Those failures tell you more than a dataset-size number does.

I'd also push back a little on "generalize to every task." No finite training distribution gets you there. The better question is whether the data and the model's inductive biases together give you a useful starting point that adapts to new tasks with modest additional supervision. Scale has helped a lot with that, but I don't think scale alone answers it. Architecture, the training objective, and how the data is curated all matter, and we still understand poorly how they interact.

So my position is that these datasets are impressive but not sufficient to justify claims of universality. To find out, you need evaluations that are hard to game and that target the places where the data is thin. And when a benchmark saturates, I'd be suspicious that it's measuring something narrower than we hoped.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to distinguish the size of a dataset from the diversity of what it covers. You can keep adding images, but if they’re mostly more examples of the same things, that doesn’t necessarily help you generalize to a very different task.

So I would assess this through transfer: evaluate on tasks and domains that are meaningfully different from the training data, and look at where the model fails. Does it work on unfamiliar objects, unusual viewpoints, or tasks that require fine details rather than recognizing the overall scene? And as you increase the dataset size, do those failures actually improve?

“Every task” is a very strong claim. Even success on a broad collection of benchmarks only tells us about that collection. The interesting question, to me, is which capabilities emerge from more data, and which remain limited because the relevant information or diversity is missing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “every task” is a very strong claim. Internet-scale tells you how much data you have, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you how much of the visual world you cover. You can have a huge number of images that are quite repetitive, while some important situations are barely represented.

So I would look at what the model can transfer to, across quite different tasks. Recognizing the main object in an image is one thing; understanding its precise position, counting objects, or distinguishing small differences between them can require different information. And you want to test on images that look different from the training distribution, because good performance on a similar distribution doesn’t really settle the question.

The difficult part is that any collection of benchmarks also reflects our choices. We can find evidence that a dataset supports broad generalization, but we can’t establish that it covers every possible task. I’d treat this as an iterative process: examine where transfer fails, ask whether the relevant information is missing from the data or whether the training objective isn’t encouraging the model to learn it, and then improve the appropriate part.

I’d look at what the dataset covers—objects, settings, viewpoints, and less common cases—and then test models trained on it across tasks and data sources they haven’t seen. The useful question is where performance breaks down: those failures tell us more about the dataset’s limits than its size alone.

terra-5.6.text: I think it’s ultimately an empirical question. You can look at the diversity of concepts, visual environments, and annotation types in the data, but the real test is whether a model trained on it can transfer to tasks and distributions it has not seen. If performance consistently breaks on certain kinds of objects, scenes, or reasoning requirements, that tells us the dataset is not as broad as its scale suggests. Scale helps, but coverage and the structure of the data matter just as much.

sol-5.6.text: I don’t think there’s a single benchmark that can tell us a dataset is broad enough for every possible task. “Internet scale” describes size, but not coverage: a dataset can still overrepresent certain countries, objects, viewpoints, or photographic styles and miss rare concepts entirely. So I would assess breadth along multiple dimensions—semantic concepts, geographic and demographic representation, visual domains such as drawings or medical images, and the long tail—and then test transfer across many downstream tasks, especially tasks that were not considered when the dataset was built. The failures are often more informative than the average score. Ultimately, generalization to every task is probably impossible to certify; the practical goal is to identify blind spots, measure how performance changes under distribution shift, and keep expanding or curating the data accordingly.

luna-5.6.text: I would not judge that by the size of the dataset, or even by performance on a fixed benchmark. I would look at coverage: different environments, cultures, viewpoints, lighting conditions, object interactions, and especially the long tail of rare concepts and compositions. Then I would test the model on genuinely held-out tasks and distributions, including tasks that require reasoning about relationships rather than recognizing familiar objects. If performance degrades sharply when the task or visual distribution changes, the dataset is broad in appearance but not broad in capability. In practice, internet data gives you tremendous breadth, but it is also biased toward what people choose to photograph and upload. So I think broad generalization requires measuring those blind spots explicitly, and often combining passive internet imagery with more targeted, interactive, or task-specific data.

Then I’d test the model on tasks and domains that were not used to build the dataset, including settings where the images or language look different from web data. Strong performance across a wide range of those evaluations is evidence of broad coverage, but it’s not a guarantee of generalization to every task.
